subject: Cloud Computing
title: Firewalls in the Cloud
description: Learn Firewalls in the Cloud in one minute.

hook.text: In the physical world, a firewall is a wall that stops fire. In the cloud, it stops unauthorized traffic.

buildup.text: Cloud firewalls — security groups and network ACLs — control which traffic can enter or leave your resources.

discovery.text: Rules are defined by IP address, port, and protocol. Allow web traffic on port 443, block everything else.

twist.text: The default rule matters most. AWS security groups deny all inbound by default — Azure NSGs may not.

climax.text: Cloud firewalls are your first line of defense. But they only work if rules are reviewed regularly.

punchline.text: A firewall is only as good as its rules. Review them often.

quiz.question: What do cloud security groups control?
options: Which network traffic is allowed to reach or leave cloud resources
Which users can log into the cloud management console
How much bandwidth each cloud resource can use

details.summary: Cloud firewalls filter traffic using security groups and network ACLs that define which ports, protocols, and IP ranges are allowed. Unlike physical firewalls, cloud firewalls are software-defined and can be applied to individual instances or entire subnets programmatically.
details.whyItMatters: Misconfigured security groups that allow unrestricted inbound access are among the most common cloud vulnerabilities. Proper firewall rules are the first line of network defense.
takeaways: Security groups and NACLs filter cloud network traffic
Default-deny rules block all traffic not explicitly allowed
Firewall rules can be managed as code for consistency

faq.question: What is the difference between security groups and NACLs?
faq.answer: Security groups are stateful and operate at the instance level, automatically allowing return traffic. Network ACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level, requiring explicit rules for both inbound and outbound. Most architectures use both layers together.

faq.question: Should all ports be closed by default?
faq.answer: Yes. Follow a default-deny approach where all inbound traffic is blocked unless explicitly permitted. Open only the specific ports needed for the service, restrict source IP ranges as narrowly as possible, and avoid using 0.0.0.0/0 for any production rules.
